chapters.title: Chapter 4: The Greeks: Reading an Option's Sensitivities

lessons.title: Using the Greeks Together: A Practical Risk Read on a Zerodha Options Position

children.text: Every Greek in this chapter was computed for one single option. A real position, and any decent broker or Sensibull-style terminal, shows Greeks for the whole book at once, and it gets there through one simple rule: Greeks add up. Add each leg's Greek if you are long it, subtract it if you are short it, and the total is the position's real, combined exposure to spot, time, volatility, and rates, all at once.
The Position: Long the Call, Short the Put

Lesson 3.4 named this structure without proving it fully: buy the 24,800 call, sell the 24,800 put, same expiry. It called this a synthetic long stock position. Here are both legs' Greeks, computed exactly as Chapter 4 built them.

body.caption: Per-leg Greeks, one lot each, same strike and expiry as Lessons 3.3 and 3.4

children.text: The position is long the call and short the put, so add the call's Greeks and subtract the put's.

body.caption: Position-level Greeks: long call minus put

body.text: Delta lands at exactly 1.00. Gamma and vega both land at exactly 0.00. That is not approximate rounding, it is algebraically guaranteed: a call's delta minus a put's delta always equals exactly 1, and the two share identical gamma and vega at the same strike and expiry, so a long-call-short-put combination cancels both completely, every single time, for any strike, volatility, or time to expiry. This position does not behave like an options bet with some stock-like flavour. Every Greek confirms it is, in every measurable way, a share of stock in disguise.

children.text: The two numbers that did not vanish, theta and rho, are not really options risk either. They are the cost of financing this synthetic share instead of buying the real one. Subtract the put's theta formula from the call's, and every term cancels except one.

body.caption: This is exactly r K e^(−rT), annualized, the interest cost of the borrowed money embedded in this structure, matching the ₹20.56 rho figure from the same underlying r K e^(−rT) term. Nothing here is time decay in the usual options sense; it is pure cost of carry.

children.text: Why This Matters for a Real Zerodha Position

Open the Greeks view on a real multi-leg position, whether on Zerodha, Sensibull, or any other options terminal, and this same check tells you what you are actually holding, regardless of what you think you built it for. Near-zero gamma and vega with delta close to 1 per lot means you are carrying stock-like directional exposure with no real convexity or volatility bet in it, whatever the individual legs look like on their own. That is a very different risk than a position with high gamma and vega, which is a genuine bet on how much Nifty moves and how implied volatility shifts, not just which direction it goes.

body.title: "I built a volatility play"
body.scenario: Rohan builds exactly this position, long the 24,800 call, short the 24,800 put, and tells a friend he has set up a bet on Nifty's volatility ahead of an upcoming event, expecting to profit if implied volatility rises.
body.prompt: Using this lesson's aggregated Greeks, explain what is actually wrong with Rohan's description of his own position.
body.modelAnswer: The position's aggregated vega is exactly 0.00, and its gamma is exactly 0.00 too. Rohan has built no volatility exposure at all; a rise or fall in implied volatility will not move this position's value through vega, because the call's and put's vega cancel completely. What he actually holds is a synthetic long stock position, with delta essentially 1.00 per lot, meaning he profits if Nifty rises and loses if it falls, just like owning the underlying directly, plus a small, steady daily financing cost from theta and a small rate sensitivity from rho. If Rohan wants a genuine volatility bet, he needs a structure with non-zero vega and gamma, such as a long straddle (long call and long put at the same strike), not one leg long and the other short.

body.title: Aggregating a multi-leg book
body.question: A trader is long 2 lots of a call with delta 0.60 and short 3 lots of a put with delta −0.35 (all in the same underlying, different strikes). What is the position's total delta?
options: 2.25, since quantities do not affect delta
body.explanation: Add each leg's delta multiplied by its quantity, with a short position's delta subtracted (equivalently, multiplied by −1 before adding). Long 2 lots at 0.60 contributes +1.20. Short 3 lots at −0.35 contributes −(3 × −0.35) = +1.05. Total: 1.20 + 1.05 = 2.25.

body.text: A single option's Greeks describe one contract. A book's Greeks, added leg by leg with the right signs, describe your actual risk. Reading them together is how you find out what a position really is, sometimes very different from what it was built to look like.

points: Portfolio Greeks are additive: sum each leg's Greek times its quantity, with short positions subtracted, to get the position's true combined exposure.

Long the 24,800 call and short the 24,800 put produces a position with delta exactly 1.00, gamma exactly 0.00, and vega exactly 0.00, an algebraic guarantee, not a coincidence of these particular numbers.
The two Greeks that survive, theta and rho, both trace back to the same r K e^(−rT) cost-of-carry term, confirming this structure is financing, not a volatility or convexity bet.
Checking a real position's aggregated Greeks tells you what risk you are actually carrying, which can differ sharply from what the position was intended or described to be.

This closes the course's full arc: a random walk (Chapter 2) became a formula through no-arbitrage replication and risk-neutral valuation (Chapters 1 and 3), and that formula's own sensitivities, the Greeks (Chapter 4), are precise enough to prove, number for number, that two options can combine into something that is simply a share of stock.

All positions, premiums, and Greek values are hypothetical, built on the same illustrative inputs as Lessons 3.3 and 3.4, not live market data.
